title: Toulmin argument builder
description: Catalogue data for the Toulmin argument builder. The page does not fetch this file; the template, example and constants are inlined in index.html and a test keeps them equal.

sources.label: Haynes et al., A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population, N Engl J Med 2009;360:491-9
Stephen Toulmin, The Uses of Argument (1958)

claim-first.warrant: What connects the reasons to the claim:

confirm.challenge: Would a sceptic accept these grounds as facts?
Does the warrant really link the grounds to the claim?
Does the backing support the warrant, not just the claim?
Does the qualifier match the strength of the evidence?
Does this argument support the essay's thesis?

hints.question: Your claim is phrased as a question. Try stating it as a position someone could disagree with.
hints.qualifier: No qualifier yet. How strong is this claim: always, usually, probably? Say so.
hints.rebuttal: No rebuttal yet. Name one condition under which the claim would fail.
hints.warrant: No warrant yet. Say why the grounds count as a reason for the claim.

parts.name: Claim
parts.def: The position you want the reader to accept.
parts.why: Everything else exists to support it, so a reader should be able to disagree with it.

parts.name: Grounds
parts.def: The facts, data or observations you offer in support.
parts.why: A claim without evidence is only an opinion.

parts.name: Warrant
parts.def: The principle that explains why the grounds count as support for the claim.
parts.why: It makes the step from evidence to claim explicit, so it can be examined.
parts.example: A man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject.

parts.name: Backing
parts.def: What supports the warrant itself: a law, rule, theory or body of evidence.
parts.why: A sceptic may accept the grounds but doubt the warrant; backing answers that doubt.
parts.example: The statutes and other legal provisions that govern British nationality.

parts.name: Qualifier
parts.def: How strong the claim is: always, usually, probably, possibly.
parts.why: It states how far you are committed, which makes the claim more honest and harder to knock down.

parts.name: Rebuttal
parts.def: The conditions under which the claim would not hold, including honest objections.
parts.why: Naming the exceptions yourself builds trust and shows you considered the other side.
parts.example: Unless both his parents were aliens, or he has become a naturalised American.

essay.title: Why every major operation should run through a checklist
essay.thesis: Every hospital should require a short written safety checklist for major operations.

arguments.label: It works
arguments.claim: Adopting a surgical safety checklist lowers deaths and complications.

grounds.text: In eight hospitals in eight cities, inpatient deaths after major surgery fell from 1.5% to 0.8% after a 19-item checklist was introduced.
grounds.source: Haynes et al., N Engl J Med 2009;360:491-9, doi:10.1056/NEJMsa0810119

grounds.text: Major complications fell from 11.0% to 7.0% in the same study, which followed 3,733 patients before and 3,955 after.
grounds.source: Haynes et al., N Engl J Med 2009;360:491-9, doi:10.1056/NEJMsa0810119

arguments.warrant: If outcomes improve across varied hospitals after a single change, that change is a likely cause.
arguments.backing: The hospitals were in both rich and poor countries, and the study's lead author reported a visible impact at every site, which makes a local fluke less likely (Harvard Gazette, 2009).
rebuttals: The study compared the same hospitals before and after, with no control group, so other changes over the same period could explain part of the improvement.
The results describe major operations in the study's hospitals; smaller or very different settings may see smaller gains.

arguments.label: It is cheap
arguments.claim: A surgical checklist is a low-cost change compared with the harm it targets.

grounds.text: The checklist has 19 items and is used at three pauses: before anaesthesia, before the incision and before the patient leaves the operating room.
grounds.source: Haynes et al., N Engl J Med 2009;360:491-9

grounds.text: The study's authors described it as neither costly nor lengthy to put into practice.
grounds.source: Haynes et al., N Engl J Med 2009;360:491-9

arguments.warrant: A measure that adds little cost and little time, and prevents costly harm, is worth requiring.
arguments.backing: Preventing a complication saves treatment, hospital days and suffering; a Harvard team estimated that universal use in US operating rooms could save $15 billion to $25 billion a year (Harvard Gazette, 2009).
rebuttals: The US savings figure is a projection from the research team, not a measured result.

arguments.label: Make it required
arguments.claim: Hospitals should require the checklist rather than leave it optional.

grounds.text: In the study, teams confirmed each checklist item aloud, and adherence to six key safety measures rose by about two-thirds.
grounds.source: Haynes et al., N Engl J Med 2009;360:491-9

grounds.text: The study's lead author said that with a checklist other team members are more likely to speak up if they see something going wrong.

arguments.warrant: A safeguard that depends on everyone using it every time loses most of its value when it is optional.
arguments.backing: Checklists like this are standard practice before every flight in aviation.

arguments.label: Harry
arguments.warrant: A man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject.
arguments.backing: The statutes and other legal provisions that govern British nationality.
rebuttals: Unless both his parents were aliens, or he has become a naturalised American.
